title: Git & Workflows
description: Commits, PRs, parallel worktrees and test-driven loops with Claude.

lessons.title: Commits & PRs
lessons.description: Let Claude handle the git chores

theory.title: Claude speaks git
theory.body:
Claude can stage files, write commit messages, commit, and open pull requests. Just ask in plain words: **"commit my changes with a descriptive message"** or **"create a pr"**.

For PRs, Claude uses the GitHub `gh` CLI, so install it and run `gh auth login` first.

Kip tip: Claude links the session to the PR it creates, so `claude --from-pr 123` finds that conversation later.
theory.code:
> summarize the changes I've made to the auth module
> commit them with a message that explains why
> create a pr

theory.title: Review the diff before it ships
theory.body:
Claude's edits can look plausible and still be wrong. Before committing, read the diff yourself (`git diff`, `git diff --staged`) or ask Claude to **review the diff for bugs, edge cases and missing tests**.

After Claude writes a PR, ask it to highlight risks you should double-check.

exercises.prompt: Which tool does Claude use to open GitHub pull requests from your terminal?
exercises.explanation: Claude creates PRs with `gh pr create`, so the GitHub CLI must be installed and authenticated.

exercises.prompt: Claude just fixed a cart total bug and you want it shipped for review.
options: Create a branch fix/cart-total, commit the fix with a message explaining the bug, and open a PR against main describing the change and how you tested it.
exercises.explanation: The better prompt keeps work off main and asks for a commit message and PR description that reviewers can use.

exercises.prompt: Order a careful ship-it flow with Claude.
steps: Ask Claude to summarize the changes you made
Ask Claude to review the diff for bugs and missing tests
Ask Claude to commit with a descriptive message
Ask Claude to create a pr
Read the PR and ask Claude to flag any risks
exercises.explanation: Summarize and review before committing, then open the PR and double-check it before reviewers see it.

exercises.prompt: In your shell, show the changes that are staged for the next commit.
exercises.explanation: `git diff --staged` (alias `--cached`) shows exactly what will go into the commit.

exercises.prompt: Why review the diff before letting Claude commit?
options: Git refuses commits without a review
Claude can't write commit messages without it
Edits can look plausible but be wrong; the diff shows exactly what changed
exercises.explanation: The diff is the ground truth of what changed, so it's where you catch subtle mistakes.

exercises.code:
> review the ___ diff for bugs and missing tests
> commit with a message explaining ___ the change was made
> create a ___
exercises.explanation: Review what's staged, ask for a message that explains why, then ask Claude to create a pr.

exercises.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
exercises.explanation: These are the commands Claude (and you) use to inspect, record and ship changes.

exercises.prompt: Claude opened PR #1234 last week. How do you jump back to that session?
exercises.explanation: `claude --from-pr` opens the session picker filtered to sessions linked to that PR.

exercises.scenario: Claude just fixed a timezone bug in the date parser and added tests. Write one prompt that gets the change reviewed, committed and opened as a PR.
exercises.sample: Review the diff for @src/utils/date.ts and @tests/date.test.ts for bugs or missing edge cases and run the tests. If they pass, commit on a new branch fix/date-timezone with a message explaining the timezone bug, then create a pr that describes the fix and how it was tested.
exercises.explanation: A strong ship prompt chains review, verification, commit and PR with clear names for the branch and the change.

theory.title: Worktrees: parallel Claudes, no collisions
theory.body:
A **git worktree** is a separate checkout of your repo on its own branch. Files are independent, git history is shared.

Run one Claude session per worktree and they can't overwrite each other's edits. Kip runs three at once and never pinches his own claw.

The repo needs at least one commit first. `claude --worktree <name>` (or `-w`) creates one for you under `.claude/worktrees/`.
theory.code:
git worktree add ../project-feature-a -b feature-a
cd ../project-feature-a && claude

git worktree list
git worktree remove ../project-feature-a

# or let Claude Code create it
claude --worktree feature-auth

theory.title: The test-driven loop
theory.body:
Tests give Claude a clear target it can check itself.

**1.** Ask Claude to write tests from expected inputs and outputs, and say you're doing TDD so it doesn't write the implementation.

**2.** Run them and confirm they **fail**. Commit the tests.

**3.** Ask Claude to write code that makes them pass **without modifying the tests**, iterating until green.

**4.** Commit the code.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to run a parallel Claude session in a worktree.
steps: Run claude and give it the feature task
Review, commit and merge the feature-a branch
exercises.explanation: Create the worktree, work in it with its own Claude, merge the branch, then clean up.

exercises.prompt: Create a worktree at ../project-feature-a on a new branch named feature-a.
exercises.explanation: `git worktree add <path> -b <branch>` makes a new checkout on a fresh branch.

exercises.prompt: Start Claude in an isolated worktree named feature-auth (let Claude Code create it).
exercises.explanation: `claude --worktree <name>` (or `-w`) creates a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` and starts there.

exercises.prompt: List all worktrees for this repository.
exercises.explanation: `git worktree list` shows every checkout and the branch it's on.

exercises.prompt: Why use worktrees for parallel Claude sessions?
options: Each has independent files but shared history, so sessions don't overwrite each other
They let two sessions share one context window
exercises.explanation: Separate working files keep concurrent edits from colliding, while commits all land in one repo.

exercises.code:
git worktree ___ ../app-bugfix -b bugfix
cd ../app-bugfix && claude
git worktree ___
git worktree ___ ../app-bugfix
exercises.explanation: add creates the worktree, list shows them, and remove cleans one up.

exercises.prompt: Order the test-driven loop with Claude.
steps: Ask Claude to write tests from expected inputs and outputs, no implementation
Run the tests and confirm they fail
Ask Claude to write code that passes without changing the tests
Iterate until green, then commit the code
exercises.explanation: Failing tests first prove the tests check something; locking them keeps Claude aiming at the real target.

exercises.prompt: You want to build slugify() test-first.
options: Write tests in tests/slugify.test.ts for slugify(): 'Hello World' -> 'hello-world', '  Trim me  ' -> 'trim-me', '' -> ''. We're doing TDD, so don't write the implementation yet. Run the tests and confirm they fail.
Write slugify and some tests for it.
exercises.explanation: Concrete input/output pairs plus an explicit 'no implementation yet' keep the TDD loop honest.

exercises.prompt: Mid-loop, Claude suggests changing a test's expected value so it passes. What should you usually do?
options: Tell Claude to keep the tests unchanged and fix the implementation
exercises.explanation: The tests encode the spec, so Claude should change the code, unless you decide the test itself is wrong.

exercises.scenario: You need parseDuration("1h30m") to return 5400 (seconds). Kick off a TDD loop with Claude.
exercises.sample: We're doing TDD. Write tests in @tests/time.test.ts for parseDuration in @src/time.ts: "1h30m" -> 5400, "45s" -> 45, "2h" -> 7200, and invalid input throws. Don't write the implementation yet. Run the tests, confirm they fail, and commit them. Then implement parseDuration until all tests pass without modifying the tests.
exercises.explanation: Concrete examples, a 'tests first' instruction and a 'don't modify tests' rule make a tight TDD prompt.

mission.title: Ship It From a Worktree
mission.intro: Spin up a parallel workspace, drive a tiny feature test-first, and ship it as a real PR.
checklist: Create a worktree: claude --worktree tiny-feature (or git worktree add ../repo-tiny -b tiny-feature)
Ask Claude to write failing tests for a small function, run them, and commit the tests
Have Claude implement the function until the tests pass without touching the tests
Ask Claude to review the git diff, then commit with a descriptive message
With gh installed and logged in, ask Claude to create a pr
mission.explanation: Worktree isolation, a TDD loop and a reviewed PR are the core of a safe Claude git workflow.

cheatsheet.description: Ask Claude to open a pull request via the gh CLI.
Authenticate the GitHub CLI so Claude can create PRs.
Show staged changes; review before committing.
Find sessions linked to a pull request.
Create a separate checkout on a new branch.
Start Claude in a new isolated worktree (short: -w).
Show all worktrees and their branches.
Delete a worktree when you're done.
Write failing tests, commit them, implement until green without editing tests.
